content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with the planners and presenters of this material, have disclosed that they do not have any financial interests or relationships with manufacturers of commercial products, suppliers of commercial services, or commercial supporters. However, there are two exceptions: Barbara Body, who is employed by LabCorp and serves on the advisory boards of Becton Dickinson, Roche Diagnostic Systems, and Roche Molecular Systems, and Nancy Strockbine, who has conducted research with Inverness Medical Innovations. The presentations will not include any discussion of the off-label use of products or products under investigational use. Additionally, there is no commercial support for this activity. Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli (STEC) infections are responsible for approximately 100,000 illnesses, 3,000 hospitalizations, and 90 deaths annually in the United States, based on the most recent estimates from 1999. The majority of reported STEC infections in the U.S. are caused by E. coli O157:H7, with an estimated 73,000 cases occurring each year. Non-O157 STEC bacteria are also significant causes of diarrheal illness in the U.S., with at least 150 serotypes associated with outbreaks and sporadic cases. Six non-O157 serogroups (O26, O45, O103, O111, O121, and O145) account for most reported non-O157 STEC infections. The toxins produced by STEC are named for their structural and functional similarity to Shiga toxins produced by Shigella dysenteriae type 1. Shiga toxin 1 (Stx1) is neutralized by antibodies against Shiga toxin, whereas Shiga toxin 2 (Stx2) is not neutralized by these antibodies but can be neutralized by homologous antibodies. STEC are also referred to as verocytotoxigenic E. coli (VTEC), and those causing human illness are also called enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC). In this report, all E. coli producing Shiga toxin are referred to as STEC. STEC serotypes are named based on their somatic (O) and flagellar (H) antigens. O157 STEC refers to strains with the O157 antigen, regardless of whether the H7 antigen is identified or Shiga toxin production is confirmed. Non-O157 STEC are referred to by their specific O antigens. STEC infections typically cause acute, often bloody diarrhea. Approximately 8% of individuals diagnosed with O157 STEC infection develop hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a life-threatening condition characterized by thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and renal failure. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a syndrome with similar signs and symptoms to HUS, is usually diagnosed in adults. When TTP follows a diarrheal illness, it is often caused by infection with O157 STEC or another STEC strain. In this report, TTP diagnosed after diarrheal illness is referred to as HUS, regardless of the patient’s age. The progression of illness to HUS depends on the virulence of the STEC strain and host factors. While most cases of diarrhea-associated HUS are linked to O157 STEC, certain non-O157 STEC strains can also lead to HUS. The virulence of non-O157 STEC is partly determined by the toxins they produce, with strains producing only Stx2 more frequently associated with HUS than those producing only Stx1 or both Stx1 and Stx2. STEC infections and HUS occur across all age groups, but the incidence of STEC infection and the risk of HUS are highest in children under 5 years of age. Although STEC infections are more common during summer months, they can occur year-round. STEC transmission occurs through the consumption of various contaminated foods, including undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized juice, raw milk, and raw produce (e.g., lettuce, spinach, and alfalfa sprouts); ingestion of contaminated water; contact with animals or their environments; and direct person-to-person transmission, such as in childcare settings. Both O157 STEC and O111 STEC have a low infectious dose (<100 organisms), while the infectious dose for other serogroups is not well established. Prompt and accurate diagnosis of STEC infection is critical because early treatment with parenteral volume expansion may reduce renal damage and improve patient outcomes. Conversely, certain treatments, such as antibiotics, may increase the risk of HUS in patients with O157 STEC infections, and antidiarrheal medications may worsen the illness. Early diagnosis can also prevent unnecessary procedures or treatments, such as surgery or corticosteroids for patients with severe abdominal pain or bloody diarrhea. Rapid laboratory diagnosis of STEC infection facilitates timely public health actions, including outbreak detection and response, and helps identify emerging STEC strains. Delayed diagnosis may lead to secondary transmission in homes, childcare settings, nursing homes, and food service establishments, as well as delayed detection of multistate outbreaks linked to widely distributed foods. Outbreaks caused by STEC with multiple serogroups or pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) patterns have been documented. All stool specimens from patients with acute community-acquired diarrhea or possible HUS should be tested for STEC. Selective testing strategies, such as testing only specimens from children, during summer months, or those with visible blood or white blood cells, may miss infections. Some patients with STEC infection do not have visibly bloody stools, and both O157 and non-O157 strains have been isolated from patients with non-bloody diarrhea. Testing should be performed as early as possible in the course of illness, as bacteria may become undetectable in stool after one week of illness, and Shiga toxin genes may be lost by the bacteria. Diarrheal stool is the ideal specimen for testing, and it should be collected as soon as possible after diarrhea begins, while the patient is acutely ill and before antibiotic treatment is administered. Rectal swabs may be used for children but may not contain sufficient stool for multiple tests. If rectal swabs are used, broth enrichment is recommended. Specimens should be transported to the laboratory as soon as possible for O157 STEC culture and Shiga toxin testing. Specimens not processed immediately should be refrigerated and ideally not held for more than 24 hours unpreserved or 48 hours in transport medium. All O157 STEC isolates and specimens in which Shiga toxin is detected but O157 STEC bacteria are not recovered should be forwarded to public health laboratories for confirmation and further testing. Non-culture assays, such as enzyme immunoassays (EIA) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR), have facilitated the diagnosis of both O157 and non-O157 STEC infections. However, non-culture assays should not replace culture, as a pure culture of the pathogen is needed for serotyping and molecular characterization, which are essential for detecting, investigating, and controlling STEC outbreaks.
